title: Paired bird surveys identify linear relative detection drift only when time varies within calibration cycles under free method intercepts
abstract: We test which paired bird surveys can separate linear detection drift from community change. With free human and recorder intercepts, relative drift is identified exactly when time has a nonzero contrast around a cycle in the pairing graph. A connected graph can fail this test. Free pair interactions require repeated pairs. Absolute drift still needs an external reference constraint. An audit of 130,303 standard BBS runs in 1966-2025 finds the same observer on the same route at 52.3% of eligible five-year endpoints, 34.4% of ten-year endpoints and 15.1% of twenty-year endpoints. A conditional CTI precision example needs 769 completed ten-year pairs for a 95% half-width of 0.005 C per decade when contrast SD is 0.05 C and the reference is known. Reference slope error adds a floor that more pairs cannot remove. These are design results and assumed-noise scenarios. We do not measure hearing drift, ecological lag or field calibration performance. Code, proof, source hashes, aggregate counts and checks are included.

display.caption: Historical same-observer endpoint fractions, synthetic design information, and precision scenarios. Error levels in the right panel are assumed, not measured. A reference constraint is needed for absolute drift.
